The Department of Defense is expanding its use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) by formalizing Palantir Technologies’ Maven system as a long-term program, signaling a shift from experimental tools to operational infrastructure.

The U.S. Army has revealed plans to merge numerous contracts into a single enterprise arrangement, which will provide volume-based discounts and the chance to acquire up to $10 billion from the software firm across a decade.
Wedbush analysts report that this enterprise agreement combines 75 individual contracts, comprising 15 primary contracts and 60 associated agreements, into a cohesive framework.
The Army stated that this initiative aims to expedite the implementation of artificial intelligence and data integration tools, while also reducing contract-related costs and streamlining procurement processes.
Describing it as 'mass U.S Army deal Wedbush emphasized that this framework enables the Army to procure and services Palant (NASDAQPLTR) on an as-needed basis, benefiting from 'volume-based discounts.'
While the contract does not obligate the Army to any specific purchase commitments, it establishes a foundation for substantial utilization of Palantir's technology over the next ten years.
Wedbush highlighted that 'this contract win follows closely after the company's inaugural billion-dollar contract,' characterizing agreement as 'positive catalyst' the Pentagon intensifies its emphasis on AI and digital modernization.

# Palantir (PLTR) vs. Lockheed Martin (LMT): A Three-Year Comparison

*All market data as of the market close on Aug 7, 2026 (after-hours). Financials are fiscal years 2023–2025. This is informational only, not investment advice.*

## 1. The big picture

These two companies are both "defense" plays, but they're very different animals:

- **Lockheed Martin** is the world's largest defense prime contractor — it builds the physical hardware (F-35 fighter jets, Patriot and THAAD missiles, satellites, radars).
- **Palantir** is a software company. It sells AI and data-integration platforms (Gotham, Foundry, AIP, and the Maven Smart System) that help the military and companies make sense of huge amounts of data.

Think of Lockheed as the company that builds the missile, and Palantir as the company that helps decide where to point it.

## 2. Financials over the last three fiscal years

| Metric (FY) | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PLTR revenue** | $2.23B | $2.87B | $4.48B |
| **PLTR operating margin** | 5% | 11% | 32% |
| **PLTR net income** | $217M | $468M | $1.63B |
| **LMT revenue** | $67.6B | $71.0B | $75.0B |
| **LMT operating margin** | 13% | 10% | 10% |
| **LMT net income** | $6.92B | $5.34B | $5.02B |

**Takeaway:** Palantir's revenue roughly doubled over three years, and it swung from thin margins to very fat ones — classic software economics. Lockheed's revenue grew about 11% total over three years, and net income actually *fell*, squeezed by program charges and cost inflation on fixed-price contracts.

## 3. Market snapshot (as of Aug 7, 2026)

| | PLTR | LMT |
|---|---|---|
| Price | $172.01 | $587.95 |
| Market cap | ~$395B | ~$136B |
| P/E ratio | 145.8 | 21.7 |
| EPS (TTM) | $1.20 | $26.48 |
| 52-week range | $106 – $208 | $424 – $692 |

Palantir now has a market cap roughly **3x** Lockheed's — despite doing about **6% of Lockheed's revenue**. That gap is the market pricing in enormous future growth for Palantir.

## 4. 2026 contract wins

**Palantir (2026):**
- **March 2026:** The Pentagon formally designated Palantir's **Maven Smart System** as a "program of record" — meaning it moves from experimental tool into the military's permanent, funded acquisition system (Reuters, Mar 20, 2026).
- Sits on top of the **$10 billion, 10-year U.S. Army Enterprise Agreement** awarded in July 2025, which consolidated 75 separate contracts into one.
- **Feb 2026:** $7.6M Australian Department of Defence deal; expanded UK Ministry of Defence work (a £240M three-year deal signed Dec 2025).
- **July 2026 (Bloomberg Government):** Palantir captured about half of the Air Force's "Commercial Solutions Opening" spending in the first half of fiscal 2026.
- Q2 2026 results (reported Aug 3, 2026): U.S. government revenue grew **90% year-over-year** to $809M in a single quarter; full-year 2026 revenue guidance raised to ~$8.15B (82% growth).

**Lockheed Martin (2026):**
- **April 2026:** $4.7B initial contract to boost production of the advanced **PAC-3 Patriot interceptor**.
- **July 2026:** That was extended into a **$59B, seven-year deal to triple Patriot missile production** (Bloomberg, Jul 29, 2026).
- **2026:** A separate **seven-year, up-to-$35B contract to quadruple THAAD missile-defense production**.
- **April 2026:** 10-year, up to **$1.9B sole-source IDIQ contract**.
- **July 2026:** $142.9M Air Force C-5 software sustainment award; $60.6M Navy AEGIS integration contract.
- Backlog hit a record **$230 billion** at the end of Q2 2026, up $64B year-over-year — book-to-bill was 3.2:1.

**The scoreboard:** Lockheed is booking bigger single-contract dollar figures (missiles are expensive), while Palantir is winning smaller but strategically sticky software awards that lock the company into the military's core AI infrastructure.

## 5. Recent analyst commentary

- **Palantir:** Analysts (William Blair, Wedbush) frame the Army Enterprise Agreement and Maven "program of record" designation as transformational — it raises switching costs and opens up cross-selling across the DoD. But even bullish notes highlight the valuation: a trailing P/E of ~146 and price-to-sales of ~50x leave "little room for execution misses" (Yahoo Finance, Jun 29, 2026). The Q2 2026 beat (revenue $1.94B vs. $1.81B expected) drove management to raise 2026 guidance by 11 percentage points.
- **Lockheed Martin:** Analysts are focused on **backlog conversion** — how quickly that $230B backlog turns into revenue. Management raised 2026 revenue guidance to $79.75–81.75B (8% growth at midpoint, up from 5% earlier) and EPS to $29.95–$30.65. The debate is whether new "commercial-style" multi-year framework agreements (like PAC-3 and THAAD) will restore the margin discipline Lockheed lost on earlier fixed-price programs.

## 6. How each is positioned in "defense AI"

**Palantir — the software layer of defense AI.**
- Sells the AI platforms (AIP, Maven) that human operators actually use to fuse intelligence, plan missions, and target adversaries.
- CEO Alex Karp and CTO Shyam Sankar have leaned hard into "sovereign AI" — letting the U.S. government own the model weights, swap frontier models in and out, and avoid vendor lock-in.
- Palantir also partners with defense-tech peers like **Anduril** (July 2025 Army Next-Generation Command and Control contract).
- Management noted their Department of War (DoD) trailing-12-month revenue is still less than 0.25% of the Pentagon's budget — i.e., they see a huge runway.

**Lockheed Martin — AI-enabled hardware and manufacturing.**
- Uses AI more as an ingredient in its products and factories: AI-enabled munitions, predictive maintenance, quality checks, and AI-informed production lines.
- CEO Jim Taiclet's stated goal is to be "America's clear leader in the defense technology segment," not just the biggest prime contractor.
- New products mentioned on the Q2 2026 call include MORFIUS (counter-drone), Sanctum, and PAC-3 ACE — all pitched as responses to how warfare is changing.
- Lockheed doesn't sell a general-purpose AI platform the way Palantir does; instead, AI is embedded in specific weapons systems and manufacturing lines.

## 7. Quick summary

| Dimension | Palantir | Lockheed Martin |
|---|---|---|
| What it sells | AI/data software | Missiles, jets, radars, ships |
| 3-yr revenue growth | ~2x | ~11% |
| 3-yr margin trend | Rapidly expanding | Slightly compressing |
| Valuation | Very expensive (P/E ~146) | Reasonable (P/E ~22) |
| 2026 signature win | Maven "program of record" (Mar 2026) | $59B Patriot deal (Jul 2026) |
| Backlog / RPO | $11.8B total deal value (Q1 2026) | $230B backlog (Q2 2026) |
| Defense-AI role | The AI operating system | AI-enabled weapons + factories |

**Bottom line for a curious observer:** Both companies are riding the same wave of rising U.S. and allied defense spending, but they benefit differently. Palantir is a high-growth, high-multiple software bet on the AI *brain* of the military. Lockheed is a lower-growth, lower-multiple industrial bet on the AI-enabled *body* — the missiles and platforms. The stock market is currently paying a big premium for Palantir's growth trajectory, while pricing Lockheed much closer to a traditional industrial.

*Sources: Perplexity Finance (quotes, financials, transcripts as of Aug 9, 2026); Reuters (Mar 20 & Feb 3, 2026); Bloomberg (Jul 29, 2026); Military.com (Mar 22, 2026); Bloomberg Government (Jul 13, 2026); Yahoo Finance (Jun 29 & Jul 7, 2026); Lockheed Martin newsroom.*
